question: What are the statutory restrictions on granting bail under the PMLA?

retrieval_configuration.retrieval_pipeline: BM25 + Dense FAISS + RRF + case aggregation + relevance filtering + authority-aware reranking

answer:
**Statutory restrictions on granting bail under the Prevention of Money‑Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA)** The PMLA imposes special, statutory conditions that must be satisfied before a person accused of an offence under the Act can be released on bail. The principal provisions are found in **Section 45** (and, for offences punishable for five‑years’ imprisonment or more, in **Section 37** as quoted in a Maharashtra High Court decision). The restrictions are **in addition to** the ordinary bail provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (CrPC). | Provision (Statute) | Restriction imposed | Illustration from the case law | |---------------------|---------------------|--------------------------------| | **Section 45(1) – “Notwithstanding anything contained in the CrPC”** | No person accused of a PMLA offence is *bailable* unless two conditions are met. | *Sarla Gupta v. Directorate of Enforcement* (Supreme Court, 7 May 2025) explains that “no person … shall be released on bail … unless— (i) the Public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose the application for such release; and (ii) where the Public Prosecutor opposes the application, the court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that he is not guilty of such offence and that he is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.” | | **Section 45(1)(ii) – Burden of proof** | When the public prosecutor opposes bail, the *accused* must satisfy the Special Court that there are “reasonable grounds” (interpreted by the Supreme Court as a *prima‑facie* ground) for believing he is not guilty and will not commit another offence. | *Sarla Gupta* (para 52) notes that “the burden on the accused to satisfy the Special Court … is an extraordinary and standalone provision which puts the burden on the accused at the stage of seeking bail.” | | **Section 45 – Exceptions** | Bail may be granted *as a matter of discretion* by the Special Court if the accused falls within any of the following categories:
• Under‑16 years of age
• Woman
• Sick or infirm
• Accused of money‑laundering a sum **less than ₹1 crore** (whether alone or with co‑accused) | Same passage in *Sarla Gupta* (Section 45) provides the “Provided that” clause allowing bail for these persons “if the Special Court so directs.” | | **Section 37 (as quoted in *Mohammad Sajid Margub Ansari v. State of Maharashtra*, 21 July 2025)** | For offences punishable with imprisonment of **five years or more**, bail is barred unless:
1. The public prosecutor is given an opportunity to oppose;
2. The court is satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing the accused is not guilty and will not commit another offence. | The judgment restates that “no person accused of an offence punishable for a term of imprisonment of 5 years or more … can be released on bail unless the conditions … are satisfied.” | | **Section 45 – Additional limitation** | The bail restrictions in clause (b) of sub‑section (1) are **in addition** to any limitations under the CrPC or any other law then in force. | *Kailash Chandra Kapri v. State of Uttar Pradesh* (Supreme Court, 29 April 2026) quotes: “The limitations on granting of bail specified in clause (b) of sub‑section (1) are in addition to the limitations under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 … or any other law for the time being in force.” | | **Section 45 – Non‑cognizance of offences under Section 4** | The Special Court cannot take cognizance of an offence punishable under Section 4 of the PMLA except on a written complaint by the Director or an authorised Government officer. | Same provision is reproduced in *Sarla Gupta* (Section 45). | ### Key take‑aways 1. **Two‑fold statutory gate‑keeping** – (i) the public prosecutor must be allowed to oppose bail; (ii) if it opposes, the court must be convinced of *reasonable (prima‑facie) grounds* that the accused is not guilty and will not re‑offend. 2. **Exception categories** – minors, women, the sick/infirm, and low‑value money‑laundering (‑ ₹1 crore) may be granted bail at the discretion of the Special Court. 3. **Higher‑threshold offences** – for offences carrying imprisonment of five years or more (Section 37), the same two conditions apply and bail is effectively barred unless they are satisfied. 4. **Supra‑CrPC character** – the PMLA’s bail restrictions operate **in addition to** the ordinary bail regime of the CrPC; they are not displaced by it. 5. **Burden on the accused** – unlike ordinary criminal law, the PMLA places the evidential burden on the accused at the bail stage (as emphasized in *Sarla Gupta*). These statutory restrictions collectively make bail under the PMLA **non‑bailable by default**, subject to the narrow exceptions and the stringent satisfaction of the two conditions laid down in Section 45 (and reinforced by Section 37 for serious offences).
